items.syllabus_item: 4.1 Introduction of perspective view and terms used in perspective drawing

body.en:
What perspective is. Plan, elevation and section show true sizes but look flat; a perspective view shows the object as the eye sees it from one station point — nearer parts larger, parallel receding edges converging. It is the presentation language of Unit 1 (client approval, brochures, sanction 3-D views) and the only drawing that a non-technical client truly 'reads'. It gives appearance, never measurements: sizes are still taken from working drawings.

The setup (draw this picture mentally before any construction). The observer's eye rests at the Station Point (SP). Between eye and object stands the transparent Picture Plane (PP) — the sheet itself imagined vertical. Visual rays from SP through every corner of the object pierce PP; joining the piercing points gives the perspective view. Everything else is bookkeeping of that one idea.

Terms — the syllabus list, each with its job.

• Ground Plane (GP) — the horizontal plane the object stands on. • Ground Line (GL) — line where PP meets GP; the baseline from which perspective heights are measured. • Horizon Line (HL) — horizontal line on PP at eye level; all vanishing points live on it. • Station Point (SP) — eye position; its distance from PP/object fixes how 'dramatic' the view is.

• Centre of Vision (CV) — point on HL directly in front of SP (foot of the perpendicular from SP to PP); centre of the view. • Vanishing Point (VP) — point on HL where the perspective images of one set of parallel horizontal edges meet; two-point perspective has VP-L and VP-R for the two wall directions. • Visual rays — straight lines SP→object point; their PP piercing is the drawn point.

• True-height / measuring line — a vertical line lying in PP (or on a corner touching PP) where heights show true size at the drawing scale; all other heights are transferred from it along vanishing lines. • Cone of vision — cone from SP of about 30°–60° apex within which the view looks natural; object parts far outside it distort (hence SP distance rules of Numerical 4.2).

Rules that never break. Vertical edges remain vertical (in two-point perspective). Horizontal edges parallel to PP remain horizontal. Every other horizontal set runs to its own VP. Objects behind PP shrink with distance; equal heights at greater depth show smaller — the visual truth and the drawing's charm.

One, two and three-point perspective (orientation). One-point: one face parallel to PP (interiors, streets) — one VP. Two-point (this syllabus): object corner turned to PP, both wall sets recede — two VPs, the standard house view. Three-point: PP inclined, verticals also vanish (looking up at towers) — outside our scope but explains why our verticals stay upright.

h.en: 4.2 Two-point perspective of small objects — steps, monuments, pedestals
h.gu: 4.2 Two-point perspective of small objects — steps, monuments, pedestals

items.syllabus_item: 4.2.1 Two Point Perspective of small objects only such as steps, monuments, pedestals

body.en:
Why small objects first. Steps, a monument block and a pedestal are all boxes with levels: once a box can be drawn in two-point perspective and heights stacked on its corner, every small object is the same construction wearing different proportions.

Construction sequence (the method to write and follow). 1) Draw GL and HL (HL at chosen eye height, say 1.5–1.7 m at scale above GL). 2) Mark CV; place VP-L and VP-R on HL as far apart as the sheet allows (wider = calmer view; closer = distortion). 3) Choose the nearest vertical corner (the height line): mark true heights on it at scale (total height, step levels). 4) From each height mark draw lines to both VPs — these bound the two receding faces. 5) Fix the plan positions: widths along the two ground directions are set by visual-ray/plan method (in sheet practice: by the plan drawn above/rotated, projecting corners down to PP, then to VPs — your lab teacher's sheet method) or, for exam-size objects, by proportional depth points transferred onto the VP lines. 6) Verticals dropped from face corners; horizontal step lines connect between VP lines. 7) Finish: thicken visible edges, lighten/hide construction lines, no dimensioning (appearance drawing).

Steps specifically. Draw the side profile of the steps on the height-line face (risers/treads at true scale on the corner plane), then run every profile corner to the opposite VP: treads become converging bands, risers vertical faces. Three drawn steps teach the whole trick — the fourth is repetition.

Monument/pedestal specifically. Stacked boxes: base slab wider, die (middle block), cap mould — each tier is one box drawn from the same VPs, its height read off the same height line. Centre the stack on the height-line corner or offset deliberately and transfer both front corners. Symmetry is judged by the eye in the view, not measured.

Judgement checks. VP too near CV → walls bulge like a fisheye photo; HL too low → you draw a worm's view (used deliberately for monuments to look grand); verticals accidentally converged → the commonest beginner fault. Keep construction lines faint but present in the exam sheet — examiners mark method.

h.en: 4.3 Two-point perspective of a single-room residential building
h.gu: 4.3 Two-point perspective of a single-room residential building

items.syllabus_item: 4.2.2 Two Point Perspective view of single room residential building

body.en:
The object. One room (say 3.6 × 3.0 m, 3.0 m high) with a front verandah on columns and two entrance steps — the exact practical-sheet building. The method of Card 4.2 grows one step: the house is a main box + verandah box + roof prism + step boxes, all sharing the same two vanishing points.

Sequence. 1) Fix HL/GL, CV, VP-L/VP-R (sheet A2 allows wide VPs — use it). 2) Nearest corner of the room as height line: mark floor, lintel (2.1 m), ceiling/roof bearing (3.0 m), parapet/eaves. 3) Run the two wall faces to the VPs; set room depth and verandah projection on the receding lines by the plan/visual-ray transfer. 4) Roof: locate ridge ends by height line (ridge height) and run eaves lines to VPs; gable triangle on the near face. 5) Openings: door/window verticals first (dropped from lintel/sill heights transferred along VP lines), then their receding tops/bottoms. 6) Verandah: front beam line to VP, columns as verticals, its roof slab thin and parallel to the main faces. 7) Steps: two boxes of Card 4.2 at the door. 8) Ground shadow line, approach path, one tree/level context; final line weights — outline thick, internal medium, construction erased/light.

Heights without a plan transfer — the height-line trick. Any height anywhere in the view is found by sliding it (along its wall's VP line) to the height-line corner, reading where it cuts, and sliding back. Sill 0.8, lintel 2.1, parapet, ridge: four marks on one vertical rule the whole building's heights.

Presentation finish. Slight ground shading below GL, sky kept empty (or 1–2 light horizontal strokes), sun-shadow direction consistent if shadows are attempted (shadow edges run to their own shadow VPs — attempt only if taught on your sheet). Title it 'PROPOSED RESIDENCE — PERSPECTIVE VIEW', scale 'not to scale', because a perspective has no single scale.

Exam framing. The syllabus CO says 'draw two-point perspective for given small objects': sheets are judged on correct VPs, verticals truly vertical, credible proportions and clean finish — construction method visible. Practise the steps object until the sequence is muscle memory; the house is then assembly, not invention.

title.en: Numerical 4.1 — How tall does the far corner appear? (height reduction behind the picture plane)
title.gu: Numerical 4.1 — How tall does the far corner appear? (height reduction behind the picture plane)

body.en:
Given. A wall corner touches the picture plane and shows its true height: 3000 mm, drawn at 1:50. An identical 3000 mm edge stands behind the picture plane such that its distance from the station point is 1.5 times the SP-to-PP distance. (Similar-triangles visual-ray model.)

Find. The perspective height of the far edge on the sheet.

Step 1. Find the drawn true height at the picture plane.

true drawn height = 3000 / 50 = 60 mm

Step 2. State the reduction ratio from similar triangles (height on PP varies inversely with distance from SP).

ratio = (SP to PP distance) / (SP to object distance) = 1 / 1.5

Step 3. Apply the ratio.

perspective height = 60 × (1 / 1.5) = 40 mm

Final answer.

╔ The equal far edge draws 40 mm high against 60 mm at the picture plane ╗

Validity check. This shrinkage is exactly what the vanishing lines do geometrically when heights are slid along VP lines from the height line (Card 4.3). Equal things draw unequal — perspective truth, and why perspectives are never scaled for sizes.

title.en: Numerical 4.2 — Choosing the station-point distance (cone of vision)
title.gu: Numerical 4.2 — Choosing the station-point distance (cone of vision)

body.en:
Given. A house frontage (overall width across the view) is 9.0 m. To keep the view natural, the half-angle of the cone of vision should not exceed about 30° (full cone ≈ 60°).

Find. The minimum distance of the station point from the centre of the object.

Step 1. Take the half-width of the object.

half width = 9.0 / 2 = 4.5 m

Step 2. Relate half-width, distance and half-angle by the right triangle at SP.

tan(30°) = 4.5 / d

Step 3. Solve for d.

d = 4.5 / tan(30°) = 4.5 / 0.577 = 7.8 m

Final answer.

╔ Keep SP at least about 7.8 m (say 8-9 m) from the object centre for this frontage ╗

Validity check. Closer SP widens the cone: corners rush to near VPs, walls bulge (fisheye fault of Card 4.2). On paper this translates to generous VP spacing; on site photography it is why building photos are taken from across the street.

q.en: What is a perspective drawing used for, and what must it never be used for?
q.gu: What is a perspective drawing used for, and what must it never be used for?

a.en: For showing the building's realistic appearance - client approval and presentation. Never for taking measurements; sizes come from working drawings.
a.gu: For showing the building's realistic appearance - client approval and presentation. Never for taking measurements; sizes come from working drawings.

q.en: Define station point and picture plane.
q.gu: Define station point and picture plane.

a.en: SP: the eye position from which the object is viewed. PP: the transparent vertical plane between eye and object on which visual rays draw the view (the sheet).
a.gu: SP: the eye position from which the object is viewed. PP: the transparent vertical plane between eye and object on which visual rays draw the view (the sheet).

q.en: Where do vanishing points lie, and how many has a two-point perspective?
q.gu: Where do vanishing points lie, and how many has a two-point perspective?

a.en: On the horizon line (eye level). Two - VP-L and VP-R, one for each of the two receding wall directions.
a.gu: On the horizon line (eye level). Two - VP-L and VP-R, one for each of the two receding wall directions.

q.en: What happens to vertical edges in a two-point perspective?
q.gu: What happens to vertical edges in a two-point perspective?

a.en: They remain vertical and parallel - only horizontal receding edges converge to VPs. (Verticals converge only in three-point perspective.)
a.gu: They remain vertical and parallel - only horizontal receding edges converge to VPs. (Verticals converge only in three-point perspective.)

q.en: What is the height (measuring) line?
q.gu: What is the height (measuring) line?

a.en: A vertical corner line touching/in the picture plane where heights show true size at scale; all other heights are transferred from it along VP lines.
a.gu: A vertical corner line touching/in the picture plane where heights show true size at scale; all other heights are transferred from it along VP lines.

q.en: Why are the two vanishing points kept far apart?
q.gu: Why are the two vanishing points kept far apart?

a.en: Close VPs widen the cone of vision and distort the view (bulging walls). Wide spacing - SP effectively farther - keeps the view natural.
a.gu: Close VPs widen the cone of vision and distort the view (bulging walls). Wide spacing - SP effectively farther - keeps the view natural.

q.en: What is the horizon line in terms of the observer?
q.gu: What is the horizon line in terms of the observer?

a.en: The line on the picture plane at the observer's eye level; it rises/falls with the chosen eye height (roughly 1.5-1.7 m at scale for a standing view).
a.gu: The line on the picture plane at the observer's eye level; it rises/falls with the chosen eye height (roughly 1.5-1.7 m at scale for a standing view).

q.en: Name two small objects prescribed for two-point perspective practice.
q.gu: Name two small objects prescribed for two-point perspective practice.

a.en: Steps and a pedestal (also monuments) - boxes with stacked levels, ideal for learning VP construction.
a.gu: Steps and a pedestal (also monuments) - boxes with stacked levels, ideal for learning VP construction.

q.en: A perspective has no scale - yet a height line 'at scale' is used. Explain.
q.gu: A perspective has no scale - yet a height line 'at scale' is used. Explain.

a.en: Only points lying in the picture plane draw true size; the height line is such a reference. Everything behind PP is proportionally reduced, so the sheet as a whole has no single scale.
a.gu: Only points lying in the picture plane draw true size; the height line is such a reference. Everything behind PP is proportionally reduced, so the sheet as a whole has no single scale.

q.en: What is the centre of vision?
q.gu: What is the centre of vision?

a.en: The point on the horizon line directly in front of the station point - the centre of the natural view and reference for VP placement.
a.gu: The point on the horizon line directly in front of the station point - the centre of the natural view and reference for VP placement.

q.en: In the house perspective, how is a window's height placed on a receding wall?
q.gu: In the house perspective, how is a window's height placed on a receding wall?

a.en: Read sill and lintel heights on the height line, run them along that wall's VP line, then drop verticals for the window sides.
a.gu: Read sill and lintel heights on the height line, run them along that wall's VP line, then drop verticals for the window sides.

q.en: State one common beginner fault in perspective sheets.
q.gu: State one common beginner fault in perspective sheets.

a.en: Converging verticals (or VPs too close causing distortion, or measuring sizes off the perspective) - any one.
a.gu: Converging verticals (or VPs too close causing distortion, or measuring sizes off the perspective) - any one.
